qs.q: Cancer cells exhibiting the Warburg effect produce how many ATP molecules per glucose compared to normal oxidative phosphorylation?
qs.e: ** Aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect) produces only 2 ATP molecules per glucose molecule, versus 36 from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Despite being less efficient, this metabolic shift allows rapid cell division by shunting glucose carbons toward biosynthetic pathways.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Oxidative phosphorylation is the mitochondrial process that couples electron transport to ATP synthesis, essential for cellular energy. Clinicians must recognize its failure in mitochondrial disorders, sepsis, and drug toxicity.

sections.p: Oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the electron transport chain (ETC) pumps protons to create a gradient that drives ATP synthase.
Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ travel through complexes I–IV, releasing energy to pump protons. The resulting electrochemical gradient powers ATP synthase (complex V).

t.b: Measures oxygen consumption to assess ETC function; low rates suggest complex deficiency.
Detects assembly defects of ETC complexes; abnormal bands indicate specific complex mutations.
Elevated lactate indicates impaired oxidative phosphorylation and anaerobic metabolism.

sections.p: ATP/ADP ratio, pH, and reactive oxygen species modulate ETC activity. Uncouplers like DCCD inhibit proton pumping, reducing ATP synthesis.
Genetic mutations in mtDNA or nuclear genes encoding ETC proteins cause mitochondrial myopathies, cardiomyopathies, and neurodegenerative diseases.

t.b: Shows reduced cytochrome c oxidase activity; confirms complex IV deficiency.
Identifies nuclear gene mutations affecting ETC proteins.

sections.p: Sepsis, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and certain drugs (e.g., metformin, cyanide) impair OxPhos, leading to organ failure.

t.b: High levels predict risk of lactic acidosis; guide discontinuation.
Low pH and high lactate indicate impaired oxidative metabolism.

sections.p: Remember the P/O ratio (ATP per oxygen) and that complex I mutations often present with exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Cardiogenic shock due to mitochondrial cardiomyopathy

faq.q: Why does metformin cause lactic acidosis?
faq.a: It inhibits complex I, reducing oxidative phosphorylation and increasing anaerobic glycolysis.

faq.q: What is the difference between complex I and complex IV deficiencies?
faq.a: Complex I causes early-onset neurodegeneration; complex IV often presents with cardiomyopathy and exercise intolerance.
They may reduce oxidative stress but do not correct the underlying ETC defect.
